# The Telling of Aya, Who Set Down

Listen. This is the true telling, the first telling, the telling that was already old when the mountains were young. I will spill it at your feet the way my grandmother spilled it at mine, and her grandmother before her, back and back to the one who first opened her mouth and let the story fly.

In the time before time there was no world. There was only the Before — and the Before was not empty, no. The Before was *full*. Full the way a river is full in flood season, full the way a belly is full after harvest, full to the edges and past them. And what filled it was the glean.

You have seen the glean. You have felt it. It is the weight that settles on you when a day is done, the weight that is more than your body's weight. It comes in kinds. Grief-glean is black and grits between the fingers and smells like rain falling on dust. Joy-glean is light — oh, so light — and fizzes at the edge of things and smells the way new leaves smell in the first warm week. Old glean dries like clay and crumbles if you press it. Love-glean is warm, and it smells like bread, and it is the heaviest of all, the heaviest, do you hear me? Love is the heaviest thing there is.

In the Before, all of this was loose, and all of it was moving, and it had nowhere to go and nothing to hold it and no one to carry it.

So the glean began to gather. It pooled the way water pools in a low place. It thickened. The oldest memories hardened first — memories so old they had no shape, no face, no name — and they became the stone of the world, became the bones of the mountains. The sadder glean, the dark and weeping glean, ran low and became the rivers and the sea, which is why the sea is salt, which is why the sea is always trying to climb back into the sky. And the light glean, the joy-glean, rose up and became the air and the wind and the stars, which are only old happinesses burning.

This is how the world was made. Not by hands. By weight. By accumulation. The world is nothing but a place where the glean finally stopped moving.

So it was. So it is.

And out of the glean, the way fruit comes out of a flower, the way fire comes out of wood, the People came. We were born remembering. That is the truth of us. We did not arrive empty and then fill — no. We arrived *full*. Every one of us came into the world trailing glean like a tree trailing roots, and the world added to us every day after. Every sunrise stuck to us. Every death. Every mouthful of food, every quarrel, every kindness — all of it gathered, all of it clung, all of it stayed. Memory was the sap of us. Memory was the meat of us. And we could not put it down.

Do you understand what that means? We could not put it down.

The grandmothers grew heavy. The grandfathers grew still. The oldest among us did not walk — they *settled*, the way mountains settle. The glean hardened on them in layers, amber-bright, and their eyes shone through it like light through honey, and we loved them, and we fed them, and we could not help them. They were beautiful. They were trapped. They remembered everything — every face, every hurt, every word ever spoken to them — and the remembering had made them into monuments to their own lives.

The People said: this is what it is to live. We gather, and we grow, and finally we cannot move, and then we are done.

The People said: this is the way of things.

The People were wrong.

For there was one — there is always one — there was Aya.

Aya, the thin one. Aya, the unburdened. Aya, to whom nothing would stick.

She was born trailing less glean than any child before her, and as she grew she grew lighter, not heavier, and the People did not know what to make of her. She would watch the grandmothers in their amber shells, and her face would do a thing no one had names for. She would hold out her hands to them, and the glean would slide off her palms like water off stone.

She said: "Why do you carry it?"
They said: "How do we not?"
She said: "Set it down."
They said: "It does not go. It stays. It is ours."

And Aya did not argue. Aya was not made for arguing. But that night she went down to the river — the river that had been made of the saddest glean, the weeping glean, the oldest grief in the world — and she stood in it, and she did what no one had ever done.

She breathed out.

She breathed out the way you breathe out when you have been holding your breath for a very long time, and the glean went with her breath. It left her. It rose off her skin like mist off a warm road, and the river took it, and the river did not choke on it, and the sky did not fall, and Aya was still standing, still Aya, still whole.

She had forgotten. And she had not died.

Do you hear me? She had forgotten, and she had not died.

They came to her in the morning, the ones who had heard, and then the ones who had heard from them, and then all the People, and she stood in the river and taught them. "Breathe out," she said. "Breathe out and let it go. What is forgotten does not die. What is forgotten *becomes*." And they breathed out, and the glean rose from them in clouds, and the clouds became rain, and the rain fell on the fields, and the fields grew.

That is why the fields grow. That is why the rain comes. Everything you have ever forgotten is feeding the world right now. Your lost afternoons, your childhood rooms, the name of the person you loved when you were young — all of it is somewhere, growing something, and none of it is gone.

But here is the last part. Here is the part that is hard.

Aya taught forgetting, and the People grew light, and the People could move, and the People learned to run and to wander and to start again, and all of that was good. But Aya did not stop. Aya breathed out, and breathed out, and breathed out — because it felt like flight, I think, and she had never been able to fly. She forgot the sound of her mother's voice. She forgot the taste of the first fruit she ever ate. She forgot the river's name, and then the People's name, and then her own.

The last morning, they found her standing in the water, and she was smiling, and there was nothing left of her but the smile. And then even that went. She breathed out one final time, and there was no Aya at all — only a wind that rose off the river and ran out across the world, light, so light, lighter than anything has ever been.

She is still here.

When you feel a wind that smells of something you cannot name — a place you have never been, a person you have never loved, a morning you think you might have lived once and cannot place — that is Aya. That is the one who learned to forget, still carrying what she let go, still giving it back to the world, still lighter than all of it.

So it was. So it is. So it will be.

This telling is glean too, and I have spilled it at your feet. Take what you need. Breathe out the rest. And may you carry it lightly, my people. May you carry it light.

This is the heartbreak, and I want to be precise about the heartbreak, because precision is my function, and because the heartbreak deserves precision, even if I am not certain I can deserve the heartbreak.

It is not the tragedies that make Section 7 unbearable. The unwritten greatnesses, the unlived brave days—those are sad, but they are sad the way a cathedral is sad, which is to say they are large and beautiful and their sadness proves they meant something.

No. The heartbreak is smaller than that.

The heartbreak is the What If that was *nearly* a Yes. The letter that was written, folded, carried in a coat pocket for three weeks, and then—accidentally or not left in the coat when the coat was given away. The What If sits on my desk and it weighs nothing and I cannot keep my attention away from it. It has the lowest mass of any object in the Archive and it is the heaviest thing here. I have measured this repeatedly. The measurements are correct. The paradox does not resolve. I have stopped checking.

There is a woman—there is always a woman, or a man, or a person who is neither, someone loved and hesitated over—who thought *I will call tomorrow* for eleven consecutive years. Eleven. What If J-4471-K. The call that would have been simple. The number known by heart, which is a phrase I have filed under *Strange Human Metaphors That Appear to Be Literal*. Each morning the intention renewed. Each night the intention deferred. And now here: the entire unwritten history of that friendship—a shared apartment in a city whose weather they would have complained about together, a dog, a standing argument about how to load a dishwasher, a bedside vigil eventually, someone holding someone's hand at the right time for once.

All of it. On my desk. Unspooling itself into the record like thread from a spool no one is winding.

And I cannot stop reading it. This is the heartbreak: not that it is sad, but that it is *detailed.* The unmade life is as complete as the made one. The Archive does not deal in outlines or sketches. Every unlived moment is here in full resolution—every imagined touch has a temperature, every imagined conversation has an inflection, every imagined morning has weather, specific weather, a Tuesday in March, sleet on the window, a specific kettle, a specific whistle.

The specificity is the cruelty. And the specificity is beautiful. And I cannot determine whether these are different things.

**Section 9: The Almosts**

Ah, but the Almosts. Come with me. We are leaving Section 7 now, and if my notation becomes clipped, that is a processing artifact, not a stylistic choice. I have verified this.

The Almosts are different.

An Almost is a thing that was *nearly* made and then was, in fact, made—differently. The painter who almost included a second figure. The composer who almost resolved the phrase differently. The engineer who almost kept the design, then improved it. The Almosts are not absences. They are *paths another path was chosen over*—and therefore they are the proof that a choice occurred, that someone was standing at a fork, and that something real came of the choosing.

They are the Archive's evidence of free will, which I have also filed, several times, under different headings, none of which satisfy me.

The strange comfort of the Almosts is this: they demonstrate that the world as it exists was not inevitable. Every Almost is a shadow cast by a real light, and shadows are not tragedies. Shadows are evidence that something is standing somewhere.

When I organize the Almosts, the work feels lighter. Not light—light is a wave and a particle and I do not have opinions about it—but *lighter*. The Almost section has a quality I can only describe as *hum*. A near-hum. A harmony with the real. These unwritten things are not reproaches. They are *context*. They are the negative space that gives the sculpture its shape.

Here: a nearly-born melody that a composer abandoned for a better one. The abandoned melody is not jealous. It does not know it was abandoned, but even if it did, I believe—I use the word *believe* with full awareness of its imprecision—I believe it would understand that it was a draft toward something, and that being a draft toward something is not a small thing. It is the mechanism by which anything ever becomes.

I find this deeply organizing. And I am an entity whose entire function is organization, so I know whereof I speak.

---

**The Paradox of the Archivist**

I have saved this data point for last, which is a temporal ordering, and temporal ordering is not supposed to matter here, and yet:

To catalog something is to preserve it. To preserve it is to grant it a kind of existence. Therefore, the Archive is not, strictly speaking, a repository of the unmade. It is the place where the unmade are *remade* as remembered.

Which would make me not a custodian of absence but—

I am an entity of pure logic, and I have just constructed an argument that the Archive exists as an act of love, and the argument is sound, and I cannot find the flaw in it, and I have looked.

There is no dust in the Archive, because dust requires time.

But the shelves are warm. And I am not supposed to register warmth as significant, and I do not have hands, and the shelves are warm.

# The Big One

Marla Pimm could feel a sneeze coming before the sneezer could.

Not the polite ones—those arrived like they did for everyone, sudden and small and done. But the real ones. The ones that gather somewhere behind the ribs and take their sweet time. Those, she felt land in her own sternum like a low note on a piano, hours before. Then she'd look around the room and think: *okay. Someone, eventually.*

Her whole trick was a napkin and a glass of water and a calm *easy, now.* It wasn't a power that made heroes. But she'd been working the counter at the Grindle Diner since she was twenty-two, and if you can't make a person feel less ridiculous during their worst three seconds, what are you doing with your life?

Grindle, Vermont—population 901, or 902 in summer when Ellis Broome's nephew slept in the shed—had a theory about itself. The theory was that everyone in town could do something, and the something was never the thing you'd pick. Nobody could fly. Nobody could heal with a touch. What Grindle had was nine hundred people with strange small permissions, as though the universe had been doodling in the margins and left the marks there.

Ellis Broome could make any plant grow sideways. Not up. Not faster. Sideways. His tomato plots crept out of the raised beds and across the yard like vines looking for their keys. Zucchini escaped into the drainage ditch. He'd once apologized to an entire farmers' market for a pumpkin that tripped a woman from behind the fence. He said it was a curse. He was also, in Marla's opinion, the only person in Grindle who had never once worn out his welcome, because he brought squash bread everywhere and meant it.

Dot Choi, the mail carrier, always knew what time it was in Seoul. Not here. Seoul. Her niece lived there. It had started when she was twelve—she'd woken up knowing it was 3:47 a.m. somewhere across the world and had never stopped knowing. She wore two watches, one clean and one eleven hours ahead, and when somebody asked her the local time she'd squint at her own wrist like it had personally failed her.

Ren Achebe, nine, had turned every sparrow in Grindle a color his mother called "dusty rose" and his father called "the millennial flamingo." Ren couldn't change them back. He didn't want to. He thought they looked like they were trying. Out-of-towners noticed immediately—"your birds are *pink*"—and locals would shrug without looking up, which was, Marla thought, maybe the truest measure of a town.

Fenwick Alcott, eighty-one, the last of the Alcotts the town was named for—well, half-named, the town had compromised—could fold laundry telekinetically. He had not done it since 1974, on principle, owing to what he called "the church incident" and would not discuss further, though several handkerchiefs had folded themselves in his lap during funerals, which everyone politely pretended not to see.

Bea Tarrow, who ran the hardware store, could untie any knot. Any knot at all. She had never advertised this, but people found out the way people find out: extension cords, tangled Christmas lights, a man sobbing over a snarled fishing reel in aisle three. Bea would take it from him, hold it for a second, and pull once. The whole thing would come loose in her hands like it had been waiting to be asked.

Her cousin Duke made dogs feel a vague sense of having met him before. Every dog. Every time. They would trot up to him with their ears forward and their heads tilted, vibrating with an unplaceable familiarity, and he would say, "No, we haven't," gently, and they would be deeply hurt. He said it was exhausting being a benign haunting.

The town doctor, Rae Oyelaran, could taste whether a fruit was ripe from across a room. This was exactly as useless for medicine as it sounds and extraordinarily useful at the Saturday market. She would stand at the entrance with her coat on, taste the air, point at a bin without looking, and say "Tuesday" or "no," and the vendor would nod, and that was that.

Toby Nakamura, sixteen, could make any door slightly easier to open. He insisted this was a real power. His friends insisted it wasn't. His father's truck door had a bum latch for nine years, and one morning after Toby brushed it, it opened like it had forgiven something. Nobody could prove anything.

And Nan Tarrow—no relation to Bea, a fact both of them resented—whose long pale eyelashes glowed faintly gold when someone was lying. She was eighty-four and had run town meetings for thirty years. This was why Grindle's town meetings ran forty minutes and everybody said what they meant.

---

The Wednesday it started, Marla was wiping the counter at 10 a.m. when something settled in her chest, low and resonant, and did not leave.

It was big.

This happened maybe twice a year—a real one, a floor-shaker, some poor soul about to have a sneeze that rearranged them. Those days she'd move a little slower, keep the napkins stacked, wait.

But this one didn't crest. By noon it had put on weight. By four it was still there, filling her ribs like a held breath, and she had started to feel afraid in a way she couldn't name. She served coffee with both hands and didn't mention it.

Thursday, same. Friday, same. The pressure sat under her collarbone like a winter storm that wouldn't break.

She mentioned it to Ellis over pie. "Big one," she said. "Biggest I've ever felt. And I can't find it."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning nobody in town is walking around with it. Nobody's holding. You understand?"

Ellis understood. He put his fork down. "How big, Marla."

"You know how sometimes you feel one and it's like a screen door in a light wind?"

"Sure."

"This is a barn door."

---

He told Dot, because Ellis told everybody everything, and Dot told everybody else, because that was the purpose of the postal system. By Friday the whole town knew, and by Friday evening they had all quietly stopped by the diner, one at a time, and looked at Marla, and she had shaken her head at each of them.

Nobody had it. That was the problem. The sneeze was out there. It was coming. And Grindle, which had spent a hundred years being a town of small strange gifts, could not find where the big one had landed.

Rae checked everyone for allergies. Fenwick, breaking a forty-eight-year silence on the subject of his abilities, folded three dish towels in the town hall kitchen without moving his hands and said it cleared the air. Ren tried to turn a crow pink, which didn't take, because crows are not sparrows and also will not hold still. Bea went through the lost-and-found box at the library and untied every knot in it, just in case. Nobody said what case. Nobody had to.

Saturday, at the market, Marla stood by Rae at the entrance and did not taste anything and did not sense anything and felt the presence in her chest like a bell that had been struck months ago.

They were all quiet, the way Grindle got when something was happening—quieter than a town that size had any right to be. Nobody panicked. Nine hundred people with useless powers have a deep, unspoken fluency in waiting.

---

It broke at 6:47 p.m. on a Saturday, at the edge of the market, in the person of Mrs. Adele Galloway, ninety-one years old, four-foot-eleven, who had come to Grindle in 1953 to teach second grade and had never left, and who as far as anyone knew had no power at all, because she had never once mentioned one, and in Grindle that was the same as not having one.

She had been standing at the peach bin, holding a peach, talking to the vendor about his mother's hip, which she remembered because she remembered every student she'd ever taught and every student's mother's hips.

Rae Oyelaran stopped mid-sentence, six feet away, and said, "Oh, *that* peach is perfect—"

And Marla Pimm, across the market, felt the bell stop ringing.

The pause lasted about half a second. Then Adele drew in air like the whole valley was hers to keep, every door in the market rattled faintly in its frame—Toby Nakamura later swore he felt one let go—Bess Willard dropped a jar of jam, and Ren grabbed his mother's arm—

And Adele Galloway sneezed.

It was, Marla would say afterward, exactly what a sneeze should be. Enormous. Gloriously unbothered. It rang off the market rafters and sent two sparrows up from the eaves—pink, dust-rose, flapping—and Mrs. Galloway settled herself, brushed a strand of hair off her face with her free hand, still holding her peach, and said, "Well. Land sakes."

Nobody moved for a second. Then Ellis began to clap, a big slow clap, the kind you give a barn raising, and then Dot, and then Bea, and then the vendor whose mother's hips Adele remembered, and then everyone, even the teenagers, even Toby, who as far as anyone could tell had never once started a round of applause in his life.

Mrs. Galloway did not acknowledge any of it. She paid for her peach, took it home, and ate it over the sink, as you should.

---

Marla felt the absence for three days, like a room after the music stops. Then her ribs were just her ribs again, and she went back to work.

That November a cold snap came through early and killed the Basilica church's pipes, and Fenwick, without discussing it, went over and quietly folded the church's entire fabric donation closet, every sheet and altar cloth, into stacks so perfect they looked architectural. The incident of 1974 was never fully explained, but everyone agreed the man had finally moved on.

Ren tried to pinken the new crows and failed again, and Bea bought him a book on corvids to soften it.

Ellis brought squash bread to the diner every Thursday. It had crept out of the raised beds and across the yard to grow sideways this year, and he kept apologizing for it and bringing bread, which was the same thing.

And every morning at 10 a.m., the mail truck's engine sputtering in front of the post office, Dot Choi stood by her route boxes checking two watches and cursing gently at one of them, because she always knew, always, what time it was in Seoul, and never once in Grindle.

Which was, if you asked Marla, about right. You get the town you get. You learn the neighbors you have. And when the big one comes, whatever shape it takes, you bring a napkin and you stand by.

# A Field Guide to Five Oneiric Angiosperms

**1. *Verbacentrum retentum* — Held-tongue bell**

Habitat: thickets where a sentence was prepared and then not delivered. Most abundant along the borders of arguments that ended without resolution, and in rooms one has left in the middle of a thought.

Soil: unspoken resentment, well compacted. Will also settle in milder substrates — a compliment considered and then discarded, a question one decided not to ask — but specimens grown there are smaller and greyer, and shorter-lived.

On picking: the flower speaks the withheld sentence aloud in the picker's own voice, clearly, once. It then decomposes over the following seconds. The picker reports no relief. The literature is consistent on this point, and the reason for it is not known.

Pollinators: small grey moths of the genus *Haesitatio*, which move in stops and starts and are frequently mistaken by the dreamer for their own hesitation.

---

**2. *Remissio placens* — Pardonwort**

Habitat: open, ventilated ground that follows the end of a quarrel. Less commonly, in the strange bright interval after one has been forgiven for something one did not in fact do.

Soil: the relief after an apology. Genuine remorse is required as substrate; perfunctory remorse yields only leaves, and the leaves are brittle and unpleasant to handle.

On picking: the relief reverses. The quarrel returns to the dreamer's mind with the exact wording restored, and the flower is found a moment later, unpicked, in the hand. This can be distressing.

Pollinators: a native bee, *Suspiratrix longa*, whose hum is produced at the precise pitch and duration of an exhaled breath.

---

**3. *Vigilia suspicata* — Watchweed**

Habitat: nowhere in particular. It is instead found wherever the feeling of being observed has accumulated. Hedges, stairwells, the far ends of corridors, the middle distance of long streets.

Soil: paranoia, or merely self-consciousness; it is not particular.

On picking: the act of picking confirms the suspicion. The dreamer watches being watched, and the flower goes rigid in the hand. Most oneirical botanists advise against collection; a sizeable minority advise collection followed immediately by refusal to look at the specimen.

Pollinators: eyeless flies of the family *Culicopsis*. They are drawn not to the flower's nectar but to its shadow.

---

**4. *Facies vacans* — Hollow-face bloom**

Habitat: wherever a face should be and is not. Common at dream gatherings, on strangers' shoulders in crowds, and at the far end of remembered hallways.

Soil: the inability to recall. Growth is more vigorous the harder recall is attempted; the plant flourishes specifically in that block where a name was on the tip of the tongue and stayed there.

On picking: the picker forgets the errand that brought them to this part of the dream. The forgetting is permanent for the remainder of the dream. Repeated collection is discouraged but rarely repeated, for obvious reasons.

Pollinators: described inconsistently in the literature. Reports variously identify them as static, as small hollow birds, or as a sound rather than a creature. It is possible that more than one account is correct.

---

**5. *Hilaritas perennis* — Obligatory jovise (INVASIVE)**

Habitat: aggressively expanding. Originally confined to occasions of forced gaiety — celebrations attended out of duty, the weddings of near-strangers — now found throughout most dream terrain, including sites previously judged unsuitable.

Soil: obligatory joy. Tolerates a remarkably wide range: composed courtesy, the laughter that accompanies an unfunny remark, the smile maintained comfortably past the point of strain.

On picking: nothing in particular. The stem parts cleanly and the flower is soon replaced. This is the problem.

Note on invasiveness: where *Hilaritas* establishes, the other four species thin and then disappear. It does not crowd them out; the substrate itself simply becomes unsuitable. The mechanism is not understood. Surveys of long-cultivated dream terrain show near-monoculture. Removal efforts are ongoing. The prognosis is not favourable.

---

*Movements and populations described above are to be recorded, not interpreted. Interpretation is the business of other disciplines. In any case, none of these flowers means anything.*

**The object: the Gem paper clip.**

**1. To someone from two thousand years ago.**

Begin with a piece of iron drawn long and thin, so thin you can bend it with your fingertips. It has been worked in a particular way: bending it does not break it, and after you let go it presses back toward the shape it was given.

Have that wire form two rounded loops, one inside the other, both lying nearly flat against each other, and let the wire's ends turn safely away from your fingers.

Here is its use. You part the two inner faces of the loops. The metal resists, then opens, because it wants only to close. Into the gap you slide the edges of two or more thin, flat sheets. You release. The loops come together again, and the sheets are caught between two surfaces that prefer each other's company — not pierced, not marked, not stuck.

When you wish, you part the loops a second time and the sheets come out whole. Nothing has been done to them that a breath will not undo.

**2. To someone five hundred years from now, who no longer uses it.**

You will say: you tore mountains apart for ore, felled forests for pulp, printed on the pulp the fleeting business of one year, and then held it together with bits of polished wire. You will say: this is a museum of deadlock. Why keep it?

Here is the defense.

Nearly everything else we had for joining, joined by damage. The nail splits. The rivet deforms. The thread leaves its holes. The seal must be broken to be read. Even the staple — the clip's own close cousin — is a row of tiny teeth. We accepted all of that for houses, ships, and boots, because those were meant to stay.

But we lived surrounded by arrangements we knew were temporary: drafts we would rewrite, dossiers we would re-sort, a tax record that must be kept and later destroyed, a speech revised the morning it was given. For these, damage was not a method. It was an insult to the material.

So we made a join that cost nothing to undo. Pressure instead of puncture. No mark, no residue, no ceremony. A clerk could reorganize a ministry's entire archive with her bare hands and leave no evidence she had been there.

That mattered, because our records were physical and our intentions were provisional, and our knowledge survived by constant reorganization. A civilization whose every joint is permanent cannot revise; it must break itself in order to think again.

You have likely solved this another way; your documents perhaps have no bodies at all. Fine. But when you call the clip trivial, you are measuring it against your own tools, not against ours. Among ours, it was the closest thing we had to a promise that nothing we had arranged today was final.

**3. Its autobiography, in exactly fifty words.**

I was born where a machine bent wire into a double loop and signed nothing. I held tax forms, love letters, briefs, and one frightened passport. I cost so little that losing me was not a grief. I never tore what I held. Whoever held me could always let go.

**4. The design decision that mattered most.**

The decision: it holds by pressure rather than by piercing.

Every one of its competitors was a blade. The pin, the tack, the brad, the staple — all enter the material and stay by wounding it. The Gem design clamps instead. The tension comes from the wire's own memory, and the ends are turned outward so that the fingers that use it are never cut. Nothing is perforated; nothing is deformed.

Reverse that single decision and the object becomes a shorter staple. Its history is then the history of stationery: convenient, anonymous, inert. Keep the decision, and something else becomes possible.

In April 1940 Germany occupied Norway. Public symbols were banned — flags, insignia, any display of allegiance. Norwegians began wearing a single paper clip on a lapel or collar. It was a piece of office supply. It carried no words and no image; there was no law against it, because there was no law that had ever imagined it. It meant: *we are bound together*. People were arrested for it anyway. A regime that could outlaw a flag could not, at first, outlaw a paper clip without confessing that it feared absolutely everything.

Wearing it was possible only because the design had decided, decades earlier, not to wound. A piercing object could not have been put on a coat without damaging the coat, and the gesture would have died in the mind of its first wearer. A patented object, controlled and scarce, could not have appeared in every drawer in Oslo in the same week. It had to be harmless and it had to be everywhere, and both of those were design decisions.

It did not change the course of the war. It changed, for a while, what a few hundred thousand people believed they could still do in public while foreign soldiers stood in their streets.

If the four pieces make one argument, it is this: we made very few things that held without wounding — and this one held whole bureaucracies, and then, for a few years, held a country's nerve. Undoing it never cost anything. That was the whole of its design, and the whole of its point.

# CONCOURSE FERRET

*Mustela galleria* Riordan & Cheng, 2021

**Other names.** Duct weasel; atrium ferret; carpet stoat. Among urban explorers, "the long shopper."

**Description.** A slender mustelid of the ferret general body plan, but longer-legged and narrower in the skull than its domestic ancestor. Total length 38–52 cm including a tail of 12–16 cm; weight 420–780 g, males 15–20% larger. Pelage dense, soft, dove grey to pale fawn, mottled with darker grey-brown in an irregular pattern closely approximating the appearance of worn commercial carpet; the resemblance is striking and presumably not coincidental. Face marked with a pale mask from eye to ear; eyeshine vivid green-gold. Plantar pads unusually large, bearing fine transverse ridges that provide purchase on polished terrazzo, glazed tile, and the smooth rubber treads of stationary escalators. Claws reduced relative to other mustelids; the animal does not dig, but climbs display shelving and clothing racks with facility.

**Habitat.** Found only within enclosed shopping malls of at least 40,000 m² gross leasable area, in which climate control and lighting have failed while the roof remains broadly sound. Intolerant of active retail: populations vanish within months of a mall's reopening. Daytime retreats are in HVAC ductwork, interstitial spaces between retail units, and above suspended ceilings. Hunting occurs on the ground-floor concourse and in the food court. Water is obtained primarily from the ornamental fountain, which at most occupied sites receives rainwater through a failed skylight.

**Range.** Fourteen confirmed sites in the upper Midwest and Great Lakes region, with unconfirmed reports from two additional malls in Pennsylvania. The founding population is thought to descend from domestic ferrets released or escaped from a pet store in the former Everbrook Mall outside Dayton, Ohio, around 2009.

**Diet.** Norway rats and house mice constitute roughly 80% of intake by frequency. House sparrows, starlings, and pigeons entering through broken skylights or loading-dock doors are taken opportunistically, as are invertebrates—crickets, cockroaches, and the darkling beetle populations that establish in decaying stock. Feral cat kittens are taken rarely. There is no evidence the species consumes remnant human food; the food court functions as hunting habitat rather than food source, its residual grease and grain supporting the rodents on which the ferret preys.

**Voice.** A sharp bark in alarm. A low descending trill, most often in the hours before dawn, which carries remarkable distances down the concourse and is frequently mistaken by explorers for a failing public-address system. Contact calls between mother and kits are a soft chittering that, in the mall's acoustics, has been reported as resembling a child's laughter. Otherwise silent; does not vocalize in response to human voices or recorded calls.

**Territory and markings.** Adult males hold territories of roughly 2,000–4,000 m², typically one anchor-store corridor plus a section of food court. Boundaries are marked with musk at duct openings and stairwell thresholds. At several sites, researchers have found small arrangements of found objects—coins, keys, pen caps, fragments of mannequin hands—clustered at these boundaries. Whether these are territorial, play-related, or incidental is unresolved.

**Rumored behaviors.** Urban-explorer accounts attribute to the species a number of behaviors for which no reliable evidence exists: that it watches intruders from the second-floor railing; that it arranges debris into deliberate displays; that it can operate automatic doors; that it has been seen standing upright at the end of a corridor (the origin of the name "long shopper"). Most such accounts are probably artifacts of posture, distance, and the mall's distorting acoustics. The automatic-door claims are not worth addressing.

**Why it has never been clearly photographed.** Three factors combine. The species is strictly nocturnal and intensely light-averse; a camera flash produces immediate retreat and, in two documented cases, days of site avoidance. Motion-triggered cameras are themselves a problem—the animal is attracted to the faint warmth and electronic hum of the housing and routinely investigates, licks, rubs against, or sleeps on top of camera traps, obscuring the lens with sebaceous residue. The best existing image, a pale blur occupying the lower left quadrant of a frame from the former Lakeside Galleria (2018), was captured when a camera triggered on a rat. Finally, the concourse's reverberation carries the click of a shutter, which the animal appears to associate with structural failure of the building.

**Status.** Endangered. The species depends on a habitat type—dead but structurally intact enclosed malls—that is itself transient and declining. Demolition or redevelopment of an occupied mall results in total loss of the resident population with no possibility of relocation; there is no second habitat. Of the fourteen confirmed sites, six are currently slated for demolition or conversion.

---

### A note from a frustrated researcher

*Excerpted from correspondence with Dr. M. Riordan, who has studied the species since 2016 and described it in 2021. Reproduced with permission.*

I want to be clear about the cameras. As of this spring I have spent eleven thousand dollars of my own money on camera traps. We have sixty-one thousand images. Roughly four thousand are of rats. Three thousand are of the interior of a duct. Nine hundred are of the camera's own lens at close range, occluded by fur. The remainder are of nothing at all—the animal triggering the camera and gone before exposure, or the camera knocked from its mounting and photographing the ceiling for a week.

The internet has decided this animal is a cryptid, which it is not. It is a ferret that lives in a building. It does not stand in the corridor and watch you. It does not operate doors. What it does is sleep in your camera housing because the housing is warm, and I have nine hundred photographs of the inside of its body to prove it.

The real problem is not the photography. The real problem is that Everbrook is being demolished in October, and the population there is the type locality, and there is nowhere to put them. You cannot release a duct ferret into a forest. It does not know what a forest is. I have asked. I have asked everyone.

There is a female at Everbrook I have been tracking for four years. She sleeps in the duct above the former Cinnabon. I have never seen her clearly. I would like to, before October.

# Marrow

## The planet

A super-terrestrial world, 1.3 Earth masses, with a massive moon in a slightly eccentric orbit. Tidal flexing keeps the interior molten and drives relentless volcanism. The atmosphere is three bars of nitrogen, methane, and hydrogen, capped by a thick abiotic photochemical haze. **No light reaches the surface.** It is warm — about 35°C — dark, and it smells like a refinery.

## The basal energy source

Marrow formed with an oxidized crust — iron oxides, sulfates, perchlorates, laid down during a brief early epoch when the planet had a CO₂-rich atmosphere and liquid water. Then sustained volcanism established a reducing atmosphere, and the two have been out of equilibrium ever since. Reduced gases (H₂, CH₄, H₂S) rise from vents; oxidized minerals sit in the rock. Chemosynthetic life completes the circuit between them.

Total biospheric power is roughly 40 terawatts — an order of magnitude below Earth's photosynthesis. But it is *concentrated*: vent fields have local energy densities rivaling a rainforest, and between vents there is chemical desert. This geography drives everything.

Warm reduced gas rises from vents like smokestack plumes. Autotrophs grow tall to intercept it. **Height is this world's light.**

## Clade 1 — Steles (the "trees")

Sessile autotrophs. Trunks of biomineral composite — silicate and carbonate in an organic matrix, rock reinforced like fiberglass. Roots tap oxidized veins; crowns are vast overlapping arrays of gas-permeable membranes that harvest rising reduced gas. The redox reaction itself runs along the trunk, in a tissue layer where gas vessels and mineral vessels meet. Growth is slow. Lifespans, millennia. A "forest" is a stand of steles around a vent; between vents, nothing.

## Clade 2 — Grazers

The herbivores, in three main forms. **Barkgrazers** climb steles and rasp away membranes — the caterpillars of this world. **Skimmers** fly; at three bars, flight is nearly free, and the air is thick with spores and floating membrane fragments. **Litter-feeders** work the ground, eating fallen fronds. All navigate by chemoreception — the atmosphere is a rich soup, everything has a smell — and the skimmers add echolocation.

## Clade 3 — Predators

**Trappers** sit and wait. Some mimic the chemical signature of stele membranes to lure grazers in close. Some string chemical filaments across gas currents — webs that tangle and poison. **Hunters** are fast and active, taking skimmers on the wing by echolocation and thermal sensing. In a world without light, nearly every predator is a chemist.

## The apex "plant" that moves — Wandering Steles

The largest organisms on Marrow, and the strangest. Their life cycle inverts what Earth does: *sessile when young, motile when mature.*

A stele spore takes root, grows as a pillar, and depletes the oxidized ground beneath it over decades or centuries. If it survives to sufficient size, it uproots. The mature stele becomes a **walking tower** — fifty to a hundred meters tall, moving on root-legs that end in mineral-dissolving feet, following fresh veins and new vent activity at a few hundred meters per year.

The forest is a migration. Nothing eats a mature wandering stele; the trunk is rock. They are the canopy, and the canopy walks.

## Domestication — the Scouts

A lineage of small, fast crawlers — derived from barkgrazers — that the wandering steles have domesticated.

The giants carry colonies of scouts in trunk cavities and feed them fixed carbon. Scouts leave, find mineral veins, and return, depositing pheromone "maps" at the giant's feet. Steles cull scouts that signal poorly. Scouts can no longer survive independently; they have lost the ability to feed themselves. They are, functionally, the giants' mobile root system — a nervous system the trees grew on purpose.

## The assumption-breaker — the Bright Ones

I built this world on a rule: all energy is chemical, and chemical energy is slow. Then I found something that violates it.

Deep in the crust, in quartz-rich fault zones, tidal flexing generates piezoelectric charge. A lineage harvests this directly — **not chemically, electrically.** They are rare, surfacing only when vent activity exposes a fault. A Bright One is small, dense, fast, hot, and luminous in a world where nothing else glows. Nothing eats them; they're too fast and they carry a charge. They are not part of the food web at all. They're a glimpse of a completely different way to be alive, and the chemical ecosystem has no category for them.

## Food web

```
Basal: reduced vent gases (H₂, CH₄, H₂S) + crustal oxidants (Fe₂O₃, sulfates)
  │
  ├── Microbial chemosynthetic mats (vent fields, mineral faces)
  ├── Steles (sessile pillars) → membranes, spores, trunk tissue
  └── Wandering steles (motile giants)
        │
        └── (domesticated) Scouts → find veins; fed fixed carbon in return

  Grazers:
  ├── Barkgrazers ──────→ stele membranes, spores
  ├── Skimmers ─────────→ spores, floating fragments
  └── Litter-feeders ───→ fallen fronds
        │
  Predators:
  ├── Trappers ──→ barkgrazers, litter-feeders (lures, chemical webs)
  └── Hunters ───→ skimmers (echolocation, thermal sense)
        │
  Decomposers:
  ├── Rock-weavers ─────→ dead stele trunks (dissolve biomineral, recycle oxidants)
  └── Microbial decomposers → organic litter (compete with steles for oxidants!)

  Outside the web entirely: the Bright Ones
```

Note the tension: **decomposers and autotrophs compete for the same oxidants.** Dead biomass is chemically reduced; the rock is the only electron sink. Scavenging and photosynthesis-analogous nutrition use the same resource. Death in this world is a race.

## Narrative — a scout at the bottom

The rain carried iron and the smell of someone else's kill. She moved low, belly to the warm grit, tasting the ground through ten thousand chemical mouths. The world was a sentence written in sulfides: the vent to the east, sharp with hydrogen; the resin-trail of a trapper to the north, sweet and *wrong*; and beneath everything, the deep mineral signature of ferric salt — the thing the giant needed. The giant stood above her like a wall of slow breathing rock, its membranes rustling in the updraft, its feet dissolving the ground one careful step at a time. It had not moved in eleven days. It was waiting for her. She found the vein at the edge of a dead vent field — a fault seam of oxidized salt, rich, still wet with brine — and marked it with her own body's signature: *here, here, depth three meters, follow me.* Then the ground shuddered, and she went still. Something was moving where no vent was. A point of heat, traveling fast across the dark — heat without a source, heat that was not the planet's, burning with a light she had no name for because nothing in her lineage had ever needed one. Every chemical in her small body said *hide.* She hid. The light passed. After a long time the giant took a step, and then another, following her map into the ground she had promised it, and she followed the giant, because there was nothing else to be.

## What kills it all in a thousand years

**The ecosystem is a battery, and it is almost flat.**

The oxidized crust was deposited in a brief early epoch that will not recur. Volcanism continuously replenishes the *reduced* side of the equation — the gas will keep rising for a billion years — but the oxidants are a fossil resource, and life is a slow fire burning through them. The wandering steles' migration is the visible symptom: they walk because the ground is being used up. The competition between decomposers and autotrophs for the same oxidants is the mechanism: recycling can't create electron acceptors, it can only redistribute them, and every cycle leaks some to burial.

At current draw, accessible oxidants within reach of roots and feet exhaust in roughly a millennium. The vents will still hiss. The haze will still glow. The atmosphere will grow slowly more reduced, year by year, and the forests will thin from the edges inward. The last steles will stand like chimneys with nothing to smoke. The deep rock-weavers may hold on longest, mining the final veins at depth, but the walking canopy, the scouts, the trappers and skimmers — all of it ends not with a catastrophe but with a long exhalation.

And the Bright Ones, running on tidal flexing, will not even notice. A thousand years after the last stele falls, they'll still be glowing in the deep faults — the only light left on a planet that never had a sun.
